specPoints.text: understand how the use of fertiliser can increase crop yield

primer.text: Fertiliser is the quiet engine of modern crop yields. This note explains why repeated harvesting strips mineral ions from farmland, how replacing them lets crops grow larger and faster, and which ions matter most — magnesium for chlorophyll, nitrate for amino acids — plus the deficiency signs that reveal them.

lessons.title: Feeding the Soil to Feed the Crop
lessons.opening: Every harvest carries mineral ions off the field inside the crop itself, so growing the same crop year after year drains the soil. Fertilisers replace those ions, letting crop plants grow faster and bigger, which lifts the yield the farmer collects.
keyPoints: Plants need a range of mineral ions from the soil to grow well.
Repeated cropping drains those ions, so they must be replaced between seasons.
Fertilisers supply the missing ions and push crops to grow faster and larger, raising yields.
Organic options include farmyard manure and compost, while chemical fertilisers arrive as dry granules or liquid sprays.

low.restatement: Crops eat the soil's minerals; fertiliser puts them back so the next crop grows bigger.
low.analogy: A repeated bank withdrawal finally needs a deposit — fertiliser is the farmer's top-up.
low.examPointer: Tie the yield gain to the growth gain: bigger, faster plants simply harvest more mass per field.

medium.restatement: Crop plants absorb mineral ions continuously, and each harvest removes them from the field; applying fertiliser, whether organic manure or chemical granules and sprays, replenishes the supply so the next crop grows faster and larger and the yield rises.
medium.analogy: Refilling the pantry after every meal cooked, so the next batch never runs short of ingredients.
medium.examPointer: Name both fertiliser families — organic and chemical — when asked how ions are replaced.

check.stem: Why do mineral ions need replacing on fields used for repeated cropping?

options.text: Each harvest removes ions stored inside the crop plants themselves
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Rain washes every ion away within a week
options.explanation: Removal happens mainly through the harvested crop.

options.text: Ions evaporate in strong sunshine
options.explanation: Ions do not evaporate from soil.

options.text: Weeds consume all ions before sowing
options.explanation: The dominant drain is the crop being taken off the field.

check.stem: How does applying fertiliser raise the yield of a crop?

options.text: Extra mineral ions let the plants grow faster and bigger
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Fertiliser kills every weed in the field
options.explanation: Weed killing is pest control, not fertiliser action.

options.text: It lowers the crop's water requirement
options.explanation: Water needs stay; nutrition improves.

options.text: It makes seeds germinate earlier each year
options.explanation: Germination timing is not the mechanism.

check.stem: Which of these is an organic fertiliser?

options.text: Farmyard manure
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Dry chemical granules
options.explanation: Granules are the chemical form.

options.text: Liquid nutrient spray made industrially
options.explanation: Industrial sprays are chemical fertilisers.

options.text: Synthetic powder blended in a factory
options.explanation: Factory-blended products are chemical, not organic.

check.stem: In which forms can chemical fertiliser be applied to a field?

options.text: As dry granules or sprayed on as liquid
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Only as gas injected into the soil
options.explanation: Gaseous application is not a taught route.

options.text: Only dissolved in irrigation channels
options.explanation: Liquid spraying is direct, not only via irrigation.

options.text: As solid blocks buried beneath roots
options.explanation: Blocks are not the described application form.

check.stem: A farmer skips fertiliser for three seasons on the same wheat field. What outcome follows?

options.text: Yields decline as the soil's mineral ion supply runs down
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Yields rise as the soil recovers naturally
options.explanation: Without replacement the supply falls, not rises.

options.text: The wheat starts making its own minerals
options.explanation: Plants absorb ions; they cannot manufacture them from nothing.

options.text: Nothing changes because ions never deplete
options.explanation: Repeated cropping demonstrably drains soil ions.

check.stem: State the purpose of adding fertiliser to agricultural soil.
check.modelAnswer: Fertiliser restores the mineral ions that crops need, so the plants grow larger and yields increase.

check.stem: Name two organic fertilisers a farmer might spread on a field.
check.modelAnswer: Farmyard manure and compost are common organic fertilisers spread on fields.

check.stem: Explain why plants cannot simply grow well without mineral ions in the soil.
check.modelAnswer: Plants depend on mineral ions to build the molecules of growth, so when ions are missing the crop cannot assemble enough new tissue and stays small and weak.

check.stem: A market gardener switches from chemical granules to compost. Explain what stays the same for the crop.
check.modelAnswer: Either source supplies the same mineral ions to the roots, so the crop still gains the nutrition that lets it grow bigger and lift its yield.

lessons.title: Mineral Ions and Their Deficiency Clues
sourceHeadings: Using fertilisers to increase crop yields
lessons.opening: Each mineral ion does a specific building job inside a plant, and each shortage writes its own symptom on the leaves. Magnesium builds chlorophyll, nitrate builds amino acids for proteins, and the exam expects both pairs learned precisely.
keyPoints: Magnesium ions are needed to build chlorophyll, and a shortage shows as yellowing leaves.
Nitrate ions are needed to build amino acids, the blocks of proteins, and shortage brings weak growth with yellowing leaves.
Phosphate supports storage and transfer chemistry, calcium strengthens walls and membranes, and potassium assists stomatal opening.
Spelling matters in the exam: crops need nitrate ions, never nitrites or nitrogen gas.

low.restatement: Magnesium makes the green stuff, nitrate makes proteins; short-change the plant and the leaves go yellow.
low.analogy: A builder short of one material — no bricks, no wall; the visible crack tells you which lorry never arrived.
low.examPointer: Learn the two required pairs as locked couples: magnesium with chlorophyll, nitrate with amino acids.

medium.restatement: Magnesium ions form part of chlorophyll, so deficient plants show yellowing leaves; nitrate ions supply the nitrogen for amino acids and therefore proteins, so deficient plants grow weakly with yellowing foliage; phosphate, calcium and potassium each underpin their own structures with distinct deficiency signs.
medium.analogy: Each ion is a key for a different workshop inside the leaf — lose one key and that workshop's output stops.
medium.examPointer: Write nitrate with care in the exam; nitrite or nitrogen loses the mark instantly.

check.stem: Which mineral ion does a plant require to build chlorophyll?

options.text: Magnesium ions
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Nitrate ions
options.explanation: Nitrate builds amino acids, not the green pigment.

options.text: Calcium ions
options.explanation: Calcium strengthens walls and membranes.

options.text: Potassium ions
options.explanation: Potassium assists stomatal opening.

check.stem: What are nitrate ions used for inside a crop plant?

options.text: Building amino acids, the units that make proteins
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Building chlorophyll molecules
options.explanation: Chlorophyll needs magnesium, not nitrate.

options.text: Opening and closing stomata
options.explanation: Stomatal movement draws on potassium.

options.text: Strengthening cell walls
options.explanation: Wall strength relies on calcium.

check.stem: A crop's oldest leaves turn yellow across the whole blade. Which deficiencies match that sign?

options.text: Both magnesium and nitrate shortage produce yellowing leaves
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Only phosphate shortage yellows leaves
options.explanation: Phosphate shortage gives poor roots and purple tinges.

options.text: Yellowing indicates calcium shortage
options.explanation: Calcium shortage deforms new leaves instead.

options.text: Yellowing means the plant has too much potassium
options.explanation: Potassium shortage yellows leaf edges, and excess is a different issue.

check.stem: Poor root growth with dark green, purple-tinged leaves points to a shortage of which ion?

options.text: Phosphate ions
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Magnesium ions
options.explanation: Magnesium shortage yellows the blades.

options.text: Nitrate ions
options.explanation: Nitrate shortage gives weak growth and yellowing.

options.text: Potassium ions
options.explanation: Potassium shortage yellows the leaf edges.

check.stem: Why is correct spelling of the nitrogen supply word critical in the exam?

options.text: Because plants absorb nitrate ions, and writing nitrite or nitrogen forfeits the mark
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because examiners deduct marks for any long word
options.explanation: Only the wrong substance name loses the mark.

options.text: Because nitrite is simply another spelling
options.explanation: Nitrite is a different ion the plant does not want.

options.text: Because nitrogen gas is absorbed by leaves
options.explanation: Leaves do not take up nitrogen gas as a nutrient.

check.stem: State the sign of magnesium deficiency in a crop plant.
check.modelAnswer: The leaves turn yellow because the plant cannot build enough chlorophyll without magnesium ions.

check.stem: Name the molecules that nitrate ions help a plant to build.
check.modelAnswer: Nitrate ions supply the basis for amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins.

check.stem: Explain why nitrate shortage weakens the growth of a whole plant rather than only its leaves.
check.modelAnswer: Proteins build every tissue, and nitrate ions feed amino acid production, so a shortage starves roots, stems and leaves alike of the protein supply needed for growth.

check.stem: A leaf test shows yellowing and the soil analysis shows low magnesium. Recommend a fertiliser choice and justify it.
check.modelAnswer: Choose a fertiliser supplying magnesium ions so the plant can rebuild chlorophyll and restore the green colour needed for strong photosynthesis.

glossary.definition: A material added to soil to replace or boost the mineral ions available to crop plants.
The mass of crop harvested from a given area of land.
Dissolved inorganic ions such as nitrate and magnesium that plants absorb from soil.
The green pigment that captures light energy for photosynthesis.
